Ladies and Gentlemen:

On September 24, 2026, the Director of the Office of Energy Projects issued a letter approving Northwest
Pipeline LLC’s (“Northwest”) request to commence the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (“FERC”
or “Commission”) pre-filing review process for Northwest’s proposed Silver Spur Project (“Project”). This
filing contains draft Resource Report 1 and a Summary of Alternatives. Northwest notes that the landowner
and stakeholder lists were filed with its September 1, 2026 pre-filing request and there are no updates at
this time.

Consistent with Section 385.2005(a) of the Commission’s regulations, the undersigned has read this filing
and knows its contents; the contents are true as stated, to the best of his knowledge and belief; and the
undersigned possesses full power and authority to sign this filing.

Consistent with Section 385.2010 of the Commission’s regulations, Northwest is serving copies of this
filing to each person whose name appears on the official service list for this proceeding.

If you have any questions regarding this filing, please contact Karen Olson at (713) 215-4232
(karen.olson@williams.com).

Respectfully,

Northwest Pipeline LLC




Joseph Dean
Director, Land & Permitting

1.0       GENERAL PROJECT DESCRIPTION

Northwest Pipeline LLC (Northwest), an indirect, wholly owned subsidiary of The Williams
Companies, Inc. (Williams), is proposing to install a new natural gas pipeline lateral to connect
the existing Northwest Pipeline in Twin Falls County, Idaho to the existing Tallgrass Energy
Partners, LP Ruby Pipeline (Ruby Pipeline) in Elko County, Nevada to provide 275,000
dekatherms per day (Dth/d) of incremental firm capacity to access supply at Opal, Wyoming with
delivery points in Idaho. The Silver Spur Project (Project) will consist of approximately 87.7 miles
of new natural gas pipeline, compressor station modifications at two existing facilities, a potential
new compressor station, and associated facilities as detailed below.
      •   Silver Spur Pipeline
          Approximately 87.7 miles of new 24-inch diameter pipeline originating at the existing Ruby
          Pipeline in Elko County, Nevada and extending to the Northwest Pipeline at MP 718.0 in
          Twin Falls County, Idaho.
      •   Buhl Compressor Station
          One new gas-fired turbine-driven compressor unit with 15,900 nominal horsepower (HP)
          at International Organization for Standardization (ISO) conditions, re-staging of two
          existing gas-fired, turbine-driven compressors, and miscellaneous piping modifications at
          the existing Buhl Compressor Station facility in Twin Falls County, Idaho.
      •   Mountain Home Compressor Station
          Two new gas-fired turbine-driven compressor units with 23,600 nominal HP at ISO
          conditions at the existing Mountain Home Compressor Station in Elmore County, Idaho to
          accommodate the removal and replacement of approximately 6,000 HP from three
          existing Ingersoll Rand gas-fired internal combustion engine-driven compressor units and
          increase the certificated station compression by 17,600 HP.
      •   Jackpot Compressor Station
          One potential new gas-fired, turbine-driven compressor station identified as the Jackpot
          Compressor Station with 4,700 HP at ISO conditions in Twin Falls County, Idaho (MP 45.9
          of the Silver Spur Pipeline).
      •   Additional Facilities
          One new Delivery Regulator Station for over pressure protection at the tie-in to the existing
          Northwest Pipeline in Twin Falls County, Idaho (MP 87.7 of the Silver Spur Pipeline / MP
          718.0 of the Northwest Pipeline)
          One new Receipt Meter Station at the connection to the existing Ruby Pipeline in Elko
          County, Nevada (MP 0.0 of the Silver Spur Pipeline / MP 273.9 of the Ruby Pipeline)
          Additional ancillary facilities, such as mainline valves (MLVs), system crossovers
          connecting the Silver Spur Pipeline to the Northwest Pipeline, cathodic protection, and
          communication facilities in Idaho and Nevada.
Northwest is seeking authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC)
under Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act and Part 157 of FERC regulations, to construct, own,
operate, and maintain the proposed Project facilities. Subject to FERC certification of the Project

1.2.4.1 Trenchless Construction Methods
Northwest is evaluating several methods of trenchless construction. These techniques may be
used in an attempt to reduce impacts associated with construction in comparison with using
conventional (trenching) construction techniques. Northwest is evaluating the benefits, risks, and
feasibility of trenchless construction methods.

Conventional Horizontal Bore
To complete a conventional horizontal bore, a pit on either side of a road or waterbody will be
excavated to provide a working area for the equipment. A boring machine will be lowered into one
pit, and a horizontal hole will be bored to a diameter slightly greater than the diameter of the pipe
(or casing, if required) at the depth of pipeline installation. The pipeline section will then be pushed
through the bore to the opposite pit. If additional pipeline sections are required to span the length
of the bore, they will be welded to the first section of the pipeline in the bore pit prior to being
pushed through. Details regarding the use and locations of proposed conventional horizontal
bores will be provided to FERC in the Draft Resource Reports (First Quarter 2027).
Horizontal Directional Drill
The Horizontal Directional Drill (HDD) method allows for trenchless construction across an area
by drilling a hole below the depth of a conventional lay, and then pulling a prefabricated section
of pipe through the hole. This method is used to avoid direct impacts on sensitive environmental
features or areas that otherwise present difficulties for standard pipeline construction. A summary
of the HDD locations for the Project is provided in the table that follows.

the reaming process is complete, a prefabricated segment of pipe would be attached to the drill
string on the exit side of the crossing, and pulled back through the hole toward the drill rig.
If an HDD drill hole would need to be abandoned and sealed, the drill hole would be filled with
drilling fluid and grout sealed for a distance of no less than 30 feet at each side of the drill hole.

1.2.4.2 Waterbody Crossing Procedures
Crossing of waterbodies will be conducted in accordance with applicable state and federal permits
and FERC Procedures. Northwest will utilize various methods for installation of the pipeline
across waterbodies, depending on waterbody classifications and flow conditions at the time of
crossing. In accordance with FERC Procedures, waterbodies will be classified as “minor,”
“intermediate,” or “major,” as follows:
    •    Minor waterbodies include all waterbodies less than or equal to 10 feet wide at the edge of
         water at the time of crossing
    •    Intermediate waterbodies include all waterbodies greater than 10 feet wide but less than or
         equal to 100 feet wide at the edge of water at the time of crossing
    •    Major waterbodies include all waterbodies greater than 100 feet wide at the edge of water
         at the time of crossing.
Proposed crossing methods for each waterbody will be provided to FERC in the Draft Resource
Reports (First Quarter 2027).

Dry-Ditch Crossing Methods
If a waterbody proposed to be crossed by a dry-ditch crossing method is dry or has no discernable
flow at the time of construction, the conventional open-cut method will be used. Northwest will be
prepared to suspend conventional open-cut construction at the crossing and switch to one of the
dry-crossing methods described below if there is discernible flow. Temporary diversion structures
and necessary construction equipment will be on-site at proposed open-cut crossings in case it
is necessary to switch to a dry-ditch crossing method. Northwest will monitor weather conditions
to anticipate the need for using a dry-ditch crossing method.

Dam and Pump Crossing Method
The dam and pump crossing method consists of diversion structures used to temporarily dam the
waterbody, which can consist of one or more of the following: imported concrete jersey barriers,
water bladder, port-a-dams, steel plates, and/or sandbags. The selection of the dam type or
material depends on the stream or waterbody depth, flow velocity, channel width, and flow type.
This method for crossing streams and waterbodies temporarily diverts stream flow around
construction area activities while maintaining downstream flow at all times. Damming structures
will be installed upstream and downstream of the proposed trench. Pumps and hoses will be used
to convey flow around the in-stream work area, discharging the water downstream of the
construction site and creating a dry work area. Multiple discharge pumps may be required to keep
the area dry and maintain adequate flow to avoid flooding of the waterbody upstream. Pumps and
hoses will be sized to accommodate flow in accordance with the applicable regulations. The
trench then will be excavated, and the pipe will be installed in the dry ditch.
While the upstream and downstream dams are being installed, the pumps will be used to divert
water around the pipeline crossing and associated workspaces. The water will be discharged to
the downstream area through an energy dissipating (or similar) device to prevent erosion and
scouring and minimize turbidity. Once the pipe is installed, the trench will be backfilled to pre-
construction contours, and stream banks will be restored prior to restoring water flow.
The following additional stipulations will apply to all dam-and-pump waterbody crossings:

Flume-Crossing Method
Flume pipe(s) will be installed over the trench prior to trenching (or during trenching if a rain event
creates flow in a dry stream channel). Flume pipes will remain in place and be maintained until
restoration of the waterbody is complete, and downstream flow will be maintained at all times. The
size and number of flumes will be determined prior to installation based on engineering
calculations and will be adequate to handle the maximum anticipated flow during the time of the
crossing. Excavation equipment located on the stream banks will work around the flume pipe
during excavation. The pipe will be threaded under the flume pipe, and the ditch will be backfilled
while flows are maintained through the flume pipe(s) and downstream. If topographic conditions
do not permit the pipe to be threaded under the flume, the flow may be temporarily pumped around
the work area while the flume is temporarily moved to allow the pipe to be lowered into the ditch.
Flume pipes will be permanently removed as part of restoration.
The following additional stipulations will apply to all flume waterbody crossings:
    •    Steel plates, sandbags, or sandbags and plastic sheeting diversion structures or

    •    Flume pipes will be properly aligned to prevent bank erosion and streambed scour;
    •    Flume pipes will not be removed during trenching, pipe laying, or initial streambed
         restoration activities; and
    •    All flume pipes and dams that are not part of the equipment bridge will be removed as soon
         as final cleanup of the streambed and bank is complete.

Temporary Diversion Channel Method (Cofferdam)
The temporary diversion channel method is another dry alternative to the conventional open-cut
method in which water flow is temporarily diverted to a designated portion of the stream channel
to allow construction activities to take place in the stream, along the banks, or beneath the active
channel. Using a temporary diversion channel involves installing the pipe using a phased
approach as presented below:
    •    Phase 1: Install a diversion dam
    •    Phase 2: Install pipeline through the dry portion of the streambed
    •    Phase 3: Construct and stabilize the diversion channel
    •    Phase 4: Adjust diversion dams to flow into the temporary diversion channel
    •    Phase 5: Install pipe through the dry portion of the streambed
    •    Phase 6: Complete stream bank restoration

Open-Cut Wet Trench Crossing Method
The open-cut wet trench crossing method involves the excavation of the pipeline trench across
the waterbody, installation of a prefabricated segment of pipeline, and backfilling of the trench
with native material. Depending upon the width of the crossing and the reach of the excavating

pipe segment will be weighted, as necessary, to provide negative buoyancy and placed below

method will be used if it is likely flow could occur during construction of the crossing.

1.9       Reliability and Safety
Project facilities will be operated and maintained in compliance with USDOT regulations (49 CFR
192), as well as the FERC Plan and FERC Procedures, FERC Certificate conditions, and
applicable federal, state, and local regulations. These regulations are intended to ensure
adequate protection for the public and to prevent natural gas facility accidents and failures.

minimize the hazard potential to the surrounding area during operation as described in the
following sections.
1.9.1 USDOT Pipe Class Locations
USDOT regulations (49 CFR 192) define four area classifications, based on population density in
the vicinity of the proposed pipeline, for the purpose of ensuring more rigorous safety
requirements for populated areas. Class locations are also used to determine pipe wall thickness,
hydrostatic test pressures, weld inspection and testing requirements, depth of cover, and
frequency of pipeline patrols and leak surveys.
Class locations are described by the following:
    •    A “class location unit” is an onshore area that extends 220 yards on either side of the
         centerline of any continuous 1-mile length of pipeline.
A Class 1 location is any class location unit that has either of the following:
    •    10 or fewer buildings intended for human occupancy, or an offshore location.
A Class 2 location is any class location unit that has more than 10 but fewer than 46 buildings
intended for human occupancy.
A Class 3 location is any class location unit that has either of the following:
    •    46 or more buildings intended for human occupancy, or
    •    An area where the pipeline lies within 100 yards of either a building or small, well-defined
         outside area (such as a playground, recreation area, outdoor theater, or other place of

10.0     ALTERNATIVES

Northwest Pipeline LLC (Northwest), an indirect, wholly owned subsidiary of The Williams
Companies, Inc. (Williams), is proposing to install a new natural gas pipeline lateral to connect
the existing Northwest Pipeline in Twin Falls County, Idaho to the existing Tallgrass Energy
Partners, LP Ruby Pipeline (Ruby Pipeline) in Elko County, Nevada to provide 275,000
dekatherms per day (Dth/d) of incremental firm capacity to access supply at Opal, Wyoming with
delivery points in Idaho. The Silver Spur Project (Project) will consist of approximately 87.7 miles
of new natural gas pipeline, compressor station modifications at two existing facilities, a potential
new compressor station, and associated facilities as detailed below.
    •    Silver Spur Pipeline
         Approximately 87.7 miles of new 24-inch diameter pipeline originating at the existing Ruby
         Pipeline in Elko County, Nevada and extending to the Northwest Pipeline at MP 718.0 in
         Twin Falls County, Idaho.
    •    Buhl Compressor Station
         One new gas-fired turbine-driven compressor unit with 15,900 nominal horsepower (HP)
         at International Organization for Standardization (ISO) conditions, re-staging of two
         existing gas-fired, turbine-driven compressors, and miscellaneous piping modifications at
         the existing Buhl Compressor Station facility in Twin Falls County, Idaho.
    •    Mountain Home Compressor Station
         Two new gas-fired turbine-driven compressor units with 23,600 nominal HP at ISO
         conditions at the existing Mountain Home Compressor Station in Elmore County, Idaho to
         accommodate the removal and replacement of approximately 6,000 HP from three
         existing Ingersoll Rand gas-fired internal combustion engine-driven compressor units and
         increase the certificated station compression by 17,600 HP.
    •    Jackpot Compressor Station
         One potential new gas-fired, turbine-driven compressor station identified as the Jackpot
         Compressor Station with 4,700 HP at ISO conditions in Twin Falls County, Idaho (MP 45.9
         of the Silver Spur Pipeline).
    •    Additional Facilities
         One new Delivery Regulator Station for over pressure protection at the tie-in to the existing
         Northwest Pipeline in Twin Falls County, Idaho (MP 87.7 of the Silver Spur Pipeline / MP
         718.0 of the Northwest Pipeline)
         One new Receipt Meter Station at the connection to the existing Ruby Pipeline in Elko
         County, Nevada (MP 0.0 of the Silver Spur Pipeline / MP 273.9 of the Ruby Pipeline)
         Additional ancillary facilities, such as mainline valves (MLVs), system crossovers
         connecting the Silver Spur Pipeline to the Northwest Pipeline, cathodic protection, and
         communication facilities in Idaho and Nevada.
Northwest is seeking authorization from the Federal Energy Regulatory Commission (FERC)
under Section 7(c) of the Natural Gas Act and Part 157 of FERC regulations, to construct, own,
operate, and maintain the proposed Project facilities. Subject to FERC certification of the Project
and receipt of the necessary permits and authorizations, Northwest anticipates construction of the

 Silver Spur Project                                                    Resource Report 10 – Alternatives



Project would commence in Fourth Quarter 2028 to meet a proposed in-service date of Second
Quarter 2030.
Resource Report 10 discusses the environmental, economic, technological, and procedural
viability of the no-action alternative, energy conservation alternatives, system alternatives, and
Project-specific alternatives considered against the Project in accordance with 18 Code of Federal
Regulation Section 380.12(l). Northwest used the results of the alternatives evaluation process to
develop and refine the scope of the Project. Information in this Resource Report that is pending
and will be updated with the Draft Resource Report filing in First Quarter 2027 is identified by gray
highlighted italics.

10.1 Proposed Action
The Project will include installation of a new pipeline in Idaho and Nevada, modifications at two
existing compressor stations, a potential new compressor station, and associated facilities. A
detailed description of the proposed action is provided in Resource Report 1 – General Project
Description.

10.2 No-Action Alternative
Under the No-Action Alternative, Northwest would not expand its system capacity with
construction of the Project to serve growing natural gas markets. The Project would not deliver
275,000 Dth/d of new gas supply to serve the customers identified in Resource Report 1 – General
Project Description.
Although selection of the No-Action Alternative would avoid potential environmental and other
impacts, the beneficial impacts of implementing the Project (such as assisting in managing
portfolio cost for end users; providing commodity price stability for end users; improving customer
system reliability; supporting economic development in the local end user communities) would not
occur. Selecting the No-Action Alternative would not meet the stated Purpose and Need for the
Project (see Resource Report 1 – General Project Description); therefore, the No-Action
Alternative is not considered a viable option.

10.3 Energy
10.3.1 Energy Conservation
Energy conservation reduces the need for natural gas and other energy sources. Although energy
conservation would reduce demand, it would not be sufficient to replace the growing need for
natural gas supplies to meet the fuel demands of power generators and local distributors.
According to the U.S. Energy Information Administration (EIA 2025a and EIA 2025b), natural gas
remains a significant component of the U.S. energy portfolio and reached record levels of
domestic consumption in 2024, primarily as a result of demand from the electric power sector.
U.S. natural gas consumption averaged a record 90.3 billion cubic feet per day in 2024, while
domestic natural gas production remained near historic levels. Natural gas also continues to
support growing electric generation requirements, industrial demand, and increasing liquefied
natural gas (LNG) exports. Although energy conservation and energy efficiency measures remain
important approaches for reducing overall energy consumption, those measures are not
anticipated to offset the substantial transportation and delivery capacity required to meet projected
market demand in the foreseeable future. Achieving demand reductions equivalent to the capacity



                                                10-2
 Silver Spur Project                                                       Resource Report 10 – Alternatives



proposed by the Project would require widespread implementation of conservation measures
across multiple consumer sectors and geographic areas. Therefore, while conservation measures
may incrementally reduce future energy requirements, energy conservation alone does not
represent a reasonable or viable alternative to the Project.
10.3.2 Alternative Energy Sources
The purpose of the Project is to provide up to 275,000 Dth/d of year-round firm transportation
capacity from supply at Opal, Wyoming to Idaho markets. As part of the alternative selection
process, other alternative energy sources, including renewable sources, and other fossil fuels
such as coal, oil, and nuclear energy were evaluated. As discussed below, these alternatives
currently cannot provide energy sources that are economically, environmentally, and technically
more feasible or practicable than the natural gas that would be provided by the Project.
10.3.2.1 Renewable Energy Sources
Renewable energy resources, including solar, wind, hydropower, geothermal, biomass, and
battery energy storage systems, continue to represent an increasingly important component of
the U.S. energy portfolio (EIA 2025a and EIA 2025b). The EIA projects continued growth in
renewable generating capacity through 2050, with solar and wind resources accounting for a
substantial portion of future electric generation additions. Renewable energy production has
substantially increased in recent years, with record levels of solar and wind generation recorded
in 2024 (EIA 2025c). Natural gas is projected to remain an important component of the energy
portfolio in the U.S. due to operational flexibility, reliability, and ability to complement intermittent
renewable generation.
While renewable energy resources are anticipated to continue satisfying a portion of future energy
demand growth, these sources are not anticipated to fully replace the specific transportation,
reliability, and operational functions provided by interstate natural gas infrastructure within the
timeframe necessary to meet the Project objectives. Renewable resources are location
dependent and may be subject to variability associated with weather conditions, seasonal
generation patterns, and available transmission infrastructure, and many applications continue to
rely on complementary generation, storage, or dispatchable energy resources to maintain system
reliability. Additionally, renewable generation does not directly replace the need for natural gas
delivered to residential, commercial, and industrial consumers for space heating, water heating,
cooking, process heating, and other end uses. Therefore, although renewable energy resources
will continue to serve an increasing role in the energy supply in the U.S., they are not considered
a reasonable stand-alone alternative to satisfy the identified market demand served by the
Project.
10.3.2.2 Coal
Coal remains an available fuel source for electric generation in the U.S. (EIA 2025c); however,
coal-fired generation generally produces greater emissions of criteria pollutants and greenhouse
gases than comparable natural gas-fired generation (USEPA 2025). In addition, coal extraction,
transportation, handling, and combustion can result in environmental impacts associated with land
disturbance, water resource impacts, waste management, and air emissions. As electric utilities
continue to modernize generation portfolios, market trends have generally favored natural gas
and renewable resources due to economic, operational, and environmental considerations (EIA
2025c).




                                                  10-3
 Silver Spur Project                                                    Resource Report 10 – Alternatives



Although coal remains capable of meeting a portion of future energy requirements, its use would
likely result in greater environmental impacts than the transportation and use of natural gas
supplied by the Project. In addition, coal does not provide the operational flexibility and lower
emissions profile associated with natural gas-fired generation. Therefore, coal is not considered
a preferred alternative for the Project.
10.3.2.3 Oil
Petroleum products continue to serve an important role in the U.S. energy sector (EIA 2025b);
however, oil is not considered a practical substitute for the natural gas transportation capacity
provided by the Project. Although oil-fired generation facilities may supplement electricity supplies
during periods of high demand, oil accounts for a relatively small portion of total U.S. electric
generation (EIA 2025c) and generally results in greater emissions of greenhouse gases and
criteria pollutants than comparable natural gas-fired facilities (USEPA 2025).
Increased reliance on oil would also require continued production, transportation, storage, and
refining activities, each of which may result in environmental impacts, including air emissions,
land disturbance, water resource impacts, and the potential for accidental releases or spills. While
oil remains an available energy source, it would not provide the same operational, economic, or
environmental advantages associated with natural gas and is therefore not considered a preferred
alternative for the Project.
10.3.2.4 Nuclear
Nuclear power provides reliable baseload electric generation and produces minimal direct
emissions of greenhouse gases and criteria pollutants during operation (EIA 2025c). As a result,
nuclear energy may be considered an environmentally beneficial generation technology when
compared to fossil fuel-based generation sources. However, development of new nuclear
generating facilities generally requires substantial capital investment, extensive licensing and
environmental review, specialized engineering and design, and lengthy construction schedules
(NRC 2025).
Although advanced reactor technologies and small modular reactors may improve future
development opportunities (NRC 2025), new nuclear generation facilities would not be capable
of meeting the identified energy and capacity requirements within the timeframe necessary to
achieve the Project objectives. Additionally, issues related to spent fuel management,
decommissioning, and long-term waste storage continue to be important considerations
associated with nuclear development. Therefore, nuclear energy is not considered a practical
alternative for the Project.

10.4 System Alternatives
System alternatives are alternatives to the proposed action that would make use of other existing,
modified, or proposed pipeline systems to meet the objectives of the Project. A system alternative
would make it unnecessary to construct all or part of the Project, although some modifications or
additions to another existing pipeline system may be required to increase its capacity, or another
entirely new system may need to be constructed. System alternatives involving modifications or
additional system facilities would also result in environmental impacts.
To be a viable system alternative to the Project, potential system alternatives must meet three
criteria:




                                                10-4
 Silver Spur Project                                                  Resource Report 10 – Alternatives



    •    The system alternative must be capable of transporting up to 275,000 Dth/d of new gas
         supply to serve the customers identified in Resource Report 1 – General Project
         Description
    •    The system alternative must be capable of transporting the required volumes within the
         same schedule as the Project (proposed in-service date of Second Quarter 2030)
    •    Use of an alternative system must be able to meet the criteria above and at the same time
         result in reduced environmental impacts when compared to the Project
Northwest owns and operates its Mainline System within the Project area. The existing Northwest
system does not have available unsubscribed capacity to serve the volume under contract for the
Project. Using hydraulic modeling, Northwest evaluated several system alternatives that utilize
pipeline looping, or a combination of pipeline looping and greenfield pipeline, to meet Project
capacity demand.
10.4.1 System Alternative A
Northwest evaluated System Alternative A as a loop-intensive alternative along the Northwest
Pipeline to meet the Project need. System Alternative A would require approximately 163.5 miles
of 24-inch-diameter looping segments along the Northwest Pipeline and additional compression
at nine existing Northwest compressor stations in Wyoming, Utah, and Idaho. System Alternative
A would require the installation of 117,248 incremental HP, bringing the total capacity to 188,519
HP, which would represent an increase of approximately 60 percent across the nine stations.
System Alternative A would also require more land disturbance and result in greater
environmental and landowner impacts and was therefore eliminated from consideration. System
Alternative A is depicted in Figure 10-1 provided in Attachment 10.A and a comparison of System
Alternative A to the Silver Spur Pipeline route is included in Table 10-1 (Attachment 10.B).
10.4.2 System Alternative B
System Alternative B would require approximately 60.0 miles of 24-inch-diameter pipeline
originating at the existing Tallgrass Ruby Pipeline Wildcat Hills Compressor Station and
connecting to the Northwest Pipeline at approximately MP 652.7 and approximately 26.1 miles of
24-inch-diameter looping segments along the Northwest Pipeline in Idaho and additional
compression at three existing Northwest compressor stations. The installation of 41,200
incremental HP would increase the total installed capacity at those stations to 74,887 HP. System
Alternative B is a more remote route compared to the Silver Spur Pipeline, with limited access
and existing infrastructure and housing. System Alternative B would require the development of
a significant number of new access roads, expansion of existing access roads, and development
of temporary housing and was therefore eliminated from consideration. System Alternative B is
depicted in Figure 10-2 provided in Attachment 10.A and a comparison of System Alternative B
to the Silver Spur Pipeline route is included in Table 10-1 (Attachment 10.B).
10.4.3 System Alternative C
System Alternative C would require approximately 71.0 miles of 24-inch-diameter pipeline
originating at the existing Ruby Pipeline Wildcat Hills Compressor Station and connecting to the
Northwest Pipeline at approximately MP 682.0 and approximately 11.8 miles of 24-inch-diameter
looping segments along the Northwest Pipeline in Idaho and additional compression at three
existing Northwest compressor stations. The installation of 41,200 incremental HP would increase
the total installed capacity at those stations to 74,887 HP. Alternative C is a more remote route



                                               10-5
 Silver Spur Project                                                    Resource Report 10 – Alternatives



compared to the Silver Spur Pipeline, with limited access and existing infrastructure and housing.
System Alternative C would require the development of a significant number of new access roads,
expansion of existing access roads, and development of temporary housing and was therefore
eliminated from consideration. System Alternative C is depicted in Figure 10-3 provided in
Attachment 10.A and a comparison of System Alternative C to the Silver Spur Pipeline route is
included in Table 10-1 (Attachment 10.B).
10.4.4 System Alternative D
Northwest considered a loop-intensive system alternative along the existing Great Basin Gas
Transmission Company (GBGT) and Northwest Reno Laterals. System Alternative D would
require approximately 69.0 miles of 20-inch-diameter loop along the Great Basin Lateral,
approximately 61.0 miles of 20-inch-diameter loop along the Northwest Reno Lateral, and
additional station reversal and compression at three existing Northwest compressor stations and
one new GBGT compressor station. Northwest was unable to secure an agreement with GBGT
to pursue this alternative. Due to the longer overall route length and the lack of a commercially
viable path forward, System Alternative D was eliminated from consideration. System Alternative
D is depicted in Figure 10-4 provided in Attachment 10.A and a comparison of System Alternative
D to the Silver Spur Pipeline route is included in Table 10-1 (Attachment 10.B).

10.5 Silver Spur Pipeline Route Alternatives
Route alternatives to the Project were evaluated to determine the preferred Project alignment that
meets the stated Purpose and Need of the Project (see Resource Report 1 – General Project
Description), while minimizing adverse environmental and socioeconomic impacts. For the
purposes of this analysis, route alternatives were categorized as one of the following:
    •    Major Route Alternative: An alignment that deviates from the proposed route for an
         extended distance (such as more than one mile) and is not typically located near the
         proposed route
    •    Route Variation: A route adjustment over a short distance to avoid a specific resource,
         to provide a safer or more efficient crossing, or to accommodate requests of landowners,
         land management agencies, or resource agencies
10.5.1 Silver Spur Pipeline Major Route Alternatives
The Silver Spur Pipeline was routed to be co-located or adjacent with existing roads, railroads,
and utility corridors to the extent practicable. Co-location was a principal design consideration for
the Silver Spur Pipeline to minimize environmental and new landowner impacts.
10.5.1.1 Major Route Alternative A
Major Route Alternative A originates at MP 13.1 in Elko County, Nevada and extends generally
along existing U.S. Highway 93 before turning northeast to the current Project alignment at MP
23.5. Major Route Alternative A would be co-located with U.S. Highway 93 for the entirety of the
route segment. The proposed route of the Silver Spur Pipeline reduces route length and
associated land disturbance and follows a proposed transmission line corridor for this portion of
the route while reducing road and railroad crossings and steep terrain. Major Route Alternative A
was not incorporated as the Project route due to the increased length of the route and associated
land disturbance, steep terrain, and increased number of road and railroad crossings.




                                                10-6
 Silver Spur Project                                                    Resource Report 10 – Alternatives



Major Route Alternative A and the current Project route are depicted in Figure 10-5 in Attachment
10.A. A general comparison of impacts associated with the current Project route and Major Route
Alternative A is provided in Table 10-2 in Attachment 10.B.
10.5.1.2 Major Route Alternative B
Major Route Alternative B originates at MP 26.4 in Elko County, Nevada and extends generally
northeast along a similar trajectory as the current Project alignment to MP 27.6. Major Route
Alternative B crosses areas of side slopes that would require specialized construction methods,
increase construction risk, and reduce long-term operational accessibility. The proposed route of
the Silver Spur Pipeline avoids crossings of side slopes but crosses a greater number of wetlands
and waterbodies associated with the Salmon Falls Creek complex. Northwest is currently
evaluating crossing the Salmon Falls Creek complex via horizontal directional drill to avoid
impacts to wetlands and waterbodies. Major Route Alternative B was not incorporated as the
Project route due to the presence of side slopes and constructability limitations.
Major Route Alternative B and the current Project route are depicted in Figure 10-6 in Attachment
10.A. A general comparison of impacts associated with the current Project route and Major Route
Alternative B is provided in Table 10-3 in Attachment 10.B.
10.5.1.3 Major Route Alternative C
Major Route Alternative C originates at MP 34.6 in Elko County, Nevada and extends generally
northeast along a similar trajectory as the current Project alignment to MP 36.4. Major Route
Alternative C crosses areas of steep terrain, includes a waterbody crossing within the waterbody
limits for an extended distance, and would impact an existing cattle pen. The proposed route of
the Silver Spur Pipeline reduces crossings of steep terrain, orients the route for a perpendicular
crossing of the waterbody, and avoids impacts to the existing cattle pen. Major Route Alternative
C was not incorporated as the Project route due to the presence of steep terrain, orientation of
the waterbody crossing, and impacts to an existing cattle pen.
Major Route Alternative C and the current Project route are depicted in Figure 10-7 in Attachment
10.A. A general comparison of impacts associated with the current Project route and Major Route
Alternative C is provided in Table 10-4 in Attachment 10.B.
10.5.1.4 Major Route Alternative D
Major Route Alternative D originates at MP 38.3 in Elko County, Nevada and extends generally
northeast along Delaplain Road, then follows a similar trajectory as the current Project alignment
to MP 44.1 before extending north then west to the current Project alignment at MP 46.2. Major
Route Alternative D crosses areas of steep terrain and a greater number of wetlands and includes
a trenched crossing of an existing reservoir. Northwest is currently evaluating crossing the existing
reservoir via horizontal directional drill to avoid impacts to the reservoir. The proposed route of
the Silver Spur Pipeline reduces crossings of steep terrain and wetlands and incorporates an
HDD crossing of the existing reservoir. Major Route Alternative D was not incorporated as the
Project route due to the presence of steep terrain, greater wetland impacts and increased
landowner impacts, and use of trenched crossing of the existing reservoir.
Major Route Alternative D and the current Project route are depicted in Figure 10-8 in Attachment
10.A. A general comparison of impacts associated with the current Project route and Major Route
Alternative D is provided in Table 10-5 in Attachment 10.B.

 Silver Spur Project                                                   Resource Report 10 – Alternatives



10.5.1.5 Major Route Alternative E
Major Route Alternative E originates at the proposed Receipt Meter Station in Elko County,
Nevada and extends generally along U.S. Highway 93 and similar trajectory as the proposed
route of the Silver Spur Pipeline to approximately MP 29.7 before extending north then northwest
to the Mountain Home Compressor Station. Major Route Alternative E was not incorporated as
the Project route due to the introduction of technically challenging crossings of both Salmon Falls
Creek and Snake River, greater effects on land use, and increased environmental and landowner
impacts. Major Route Alternative E and the current Project route are depicted in Figure 10-9 in
Attachment 10.A. A general comparison of impacts associated with the current Project route and
Major Route Alternative E is provided in Table 10-6 in Attachment 10.B.
10.5.1.6 Major Route Alternative F
Major Route Alternative F would fully replace the proposed Silver Spur Pipeline route by
originating at a different location along the existing Ruby Pipeline in Elko County, Nevada and
extending generally north-northwest to a different location along the existing Northwest Pipeline.
Impacts associated with pipeline construction of Major Route Alternative F are generally similar
to impacts associated with the Silver Spur Pipeline. Major Route Alternative F was not
incorporated as the Project pipeline route due to the number of access roads and the anticipated
length of new roads required for construction compared to the Silver Spur Pipeline, which parallels
U.S. Highway 93 for most of the route. Major Route Alternative F and the current Project route
are depicted in Figure 10-10 in Attachment 10.A. A general comparison of impacts associated
with the current Project route and Major Route Alternative F is provided in Table 10-7 in
Attachment 10.B.
10.5.2 Silver Spur Pipeline Route Variations
Northwest is continuing to evaluate potential Route Variations for the Project. Route Variations
identified through ongoing agency, landowner, tribal, and stakeholder consultation will be
provided to FERC in the Draft Resource Reports (First Quarter 2027).

10.6 Buhl Compressor Station Alternatives
Northwest evaluated the addition of pipeline looping along the existing Northwest Pipeline as an
alternative to the proposed addition of one new gas-fired turbine-driven compressor unit and re-
staging of two existing gas-fired, turbine-driven compressors at the Buhl Compressor Station. A
pipeline looping alternative would require 12.3 miles of new 30-inch pipeline from the new Silver
Spur connection on NWP to Buhl Compressor Station. With the restaging of both the existing
units based on gas flow modeling of the system. A pipeline looping alternative would have a
greater effect on land use requirements and increase environmental and landowner impacts of
the Project, and was therefore eliminated from consideration.
An additional alternative to modifications at the existing compressor station is the construction of
a new compressor station with comparable HP located near the existing Buhl Compressor Station.
Construction of a new compressor station would result in greater effects on land use and increase
environmental impacts of the Project. In addition, the associated increase in costs would make
the Project economically infeasible for the customers. Performing modifications at the existing
compressor station will reduce land impacts.

10.7 Mountain Home Compressor Station Alternatives
Northwest evaluated the addition of pipeline looping along the existing Northwest Pipeline as an
alternative to the proposed addition of two new gas-fired turbine-driven compressor units at the
Mountain Home Compressor Station. A pipeline looping alternative would require 62.7 miles of
new 30-inch pipeline from the Buhl Compressor Station past the Mountain Home Compressor
Station based on gas flow modeling of the system. Additionally, the replacement of the less energy
efficient gas-fired reciprocating driven compressors will reduce current permitted emissions at the
station. A pipeline looping alternative would have a greater effect on land use requirements and
increase environmental and landowner impacts of the Project, and was therefore eliminated from
consideration.

10.8 Jackpot Compressor Station Alternatives
The potential Jackpot Compressor Station has been located as far north of the Receipt Meter
Station as hydraulically feasible, to support operational access, and to avoid construction in
open / undeveloped areas along the Silver Spur Pipeline route. The location provides the
following access and constructability characteristics:
    •    Existing highway and local road access, which reduces the need for constructing
         significant new permanent access roads
    •    General flat topography, which reduces cut / fill impacts and extensive site grading
    •    Proximity to existing three-phase power infrastructure, which limits construction of energy
         infrastructure to the site.
The potential Jackpot Compressor Station site was identified as meeting the operational
requirements of the Project while limiting additional land and supporting infrastructure impacts.
Northwest is continuing to evaluate the operational details of the potential Jackpot Compressor
Station based on the current transportation capacity subscribed to the Project. Additional
information regarding the potential Jackpot Compressor Station and alternatives will be provided
to FERC in the Draft Resource Reports (First Quarter 2027).

10.9 Conclusions
Project facilities and site locations are the most appropriate to accomplish the Project Purpose
and Need for the reasons discussed in the preceding sections. The total land area impacted by
the Project will be minimized by the Silver Spur Pipeline being co-located or adjacent with existing
roads, railroads, and utilities. This co-location has several inherent engineering, construction,
long-term operations and maintenance, and environmental advantages. In addition, compressor
station modifications either occur within existing facility boundaries or only occur within the area
needed to safely construct the Project. The potential new compressor station was sited to reduce
impacts to the extent practicable. Construction of the Project as proposed is considered by
Northwest to be preferable from an environmental and economic standpoint. With implementation
of appropriate mitigation measures, the Project location and actions are not anticipated to result
in significant environmental impacts.
Northwest is continuing to evaluate Major Route Alternatives and Route Variations, and
Construction Methodology to minimize impacts. Additional information regarding Project
alternatives will be provided to FERC in the Draft Resource Reports (First Quarter 2027).
